title: Shaping Future Transport Systems
text:
“Shared micromobility schemes, such as shared bikes and e-scooters, offer a flexible transport option for short-distance trips by allowing access to micromobility on an as needed basis. These schemes have the potential to contribute to transport sustainability, for example, by promoting transport equity if they are priced affordably and offer alternatives for people with limited mobility resources or for those living in areas with poor accessibility. However, they can also reinforce existing inequities when infrastructure, pricing, deployment, or patterns of use favour certain groups or areas, or when users experience unequal benefits despite having similar access, which can in turn hinder progress towards a more sustainable transport system.”
Using evidence, discuss the challenges and opportunities that shared micromobility schemes present in relation to transport equity, and how these schemes should develop to support a more equitable transport system.
The schemes of shared micromobility, a service that is present for around half a century, has sharply increased worldwide with the exploded popularity of app-based shared bike, dockless e-scooters and e-bicycles programs (Brown and Howell 2025). These systems assured a variety of urban benefits, including ‘flexible mobility, emission reductions, physical activity benefits, reduced congestion and fuel use, individual financial savings and support for multimodal transport connections’ (Fishman, Washington, and Haworth 2012, 686). As a result, shared micromobility offer a potential solution to bridge the gaps in existing transport poverty by connecting users to public transportation services.
However, the distribution of these services is not automatically accessible to all users. The policy and regulation capacity has been outpaced by the rapid growth of shared micromobility services, making it difficult to provide accessibility for all residents. The potential that shared micromobility have in order to combat transport and accessibility poverty will be addressed in three key opportunities: use of electric micromobility to reduce physical limitations, implement specific policies to ensure socio-demographic and spatial equity, and adapting shared micromobility to the context of developing countries.
One opportunity lies in the continued implementation of technology. Traditional bike-sharing systems, while beneficial, have highlighted the challenge of making them inclusive. As Guan et al. emphasises, users of conventional bike-sharing systems tend to be mostly men, young, with higher levels of education and income (Guan et al. 2024). Hence, a segment of the population, including minorities, women, and older adults, has been excluded. The growing use of shared electric micromobility, such as e-bikes, e-scooters and e-mopeds, directly addresses this issue. Therefore, by requiring less physical effort and offering greater speed, these electric options significantly increase users’ autonomy.
For this reason, shared e-scooter users can be considered more representative of the population compared to traditional bikeshare members (Guan et al. 2024).This technological implementation is fundamental to reduce physical barriers and makes shared micromobility an alternative for users with physical limitations, age, safety or trip distance concerns. However, for its effective implementation, governments must ‘introduce new policies related to maximum speeds, the mandatory use of bike infrastructure [and] the need for designated parking in service areas’ (Zakhem and Smith-Colin 2021).
Besides the physical barrier to use the shared micromobility services, there are socioeconomic and spatial gaps that prevent equity in these mobility schemes. To achieve a scenario where services benefit users equitably, it is essential to identify disadvantaged groups and implement targeted policies to improve their current situation. In this regard, the socioeconomic factor is an important barrier. Currently, many shared micromobility schemes rely on app-based and credit cards payments, leading to the exclusion to potential unbanked and low-income users. Some authorities are aware of this situation and have started requiring operators to offer smartphone alternatives and cash payment options (Brown and Howell 2025). Furthermore, the price itself is a barrier for low-income residents. The implementation of regulatory policies can reduce the current gap by offering a wide range of options to groups identified as low-income users (e.g. 30 minutes free rides or 50% fare reduction) (Brown and Howell 2024).
Moreover, spatial inequity represents another obstacle to shared micromobility accessibility. Without the planification of bikeshare stations, and especially the vehicle fleets of dockless schemes, these services tend to concentrate in affluent, centric, or high-density areas, leaving users underserved with low connectivity who could potentially benefit the most (Brown and Howell 2024). A way to mitigate this is through city authorities, which, as part of policy regulations, can require operators to allocate a fixed percentage of their fleet or stations to identified low-income or underserved areas. However, this distribution and these specifications must be properly studied for each context. A study from Su et al., has identified that ‘low-income neighbourhoods have a relatively higher demand for shared bikes but not for shared e-scooters’ (Su, Yan, and Zhao 2024, 33). This finding highlights that behaviour and decisions from the users must be considered when planning shared micromobility regulations. It also underscores the necessity of data-driven decision making.
Data collection from shared micromobility operators can be indispensable for its successful regulation. Governments can require operators to share anonymized user information to make a range of data-driven decisions. This data allows city authorities to understand user needs, identify service gaps, and develop solutions to reduce inequity. Furthermore, data can bring opportunities for decisions related to emissions, scarce travel connectivity, and accessibility (Brown and Howell 2024). In that regard, the use of data can drive improvements in the equity and accessibility of shared micromobility services.
This potential for an equitable, data-driven approach is particularly evident in cities in developing countries, especially in Latin America. These cities present a different context than those in North America or Europe. The World Resources Institute depicts that car ownership in Latin America is drastically lower, and in average a 70% less than in the United States (2024). Also, as shown in figure 1, the primary modes of transport in Latin America cities are walking and public transport. In this context, shared micromobility is not competing with the private car, but rather reinforces existing modes of transport (walking and public transport) and presents itself as an alternative for longer trips, potentially replacing the car use in this scenario. This presents an enormous opportunity, where it must be considered that the main challenge for accessibility in Latin American cities is connectivity and equitable distribution in the city, from the periphery to the urban centre, often compromised by a history of informal, unsafe, or unreliable transportation system.



Figure 1: Main modes of transport in Latin America (World Resources Institute, 2024)


In conclusion, the rapid growth of shared micromobility services represents an alternative in urban mobility, offering flexibility and reduced emissions. However, this growth has created some inequalities because the service has been prioritised for certain sectors of society and promoting a shared micromobility equity relies on the actions and regulations made by city authorities. This can be achieved by developing accessible regulations for the implementation of electric vehicles (e.g. e-scooters, e-bikes and e-mopeds) as an alternative to reduce physical limitation to users. Also, applying specific policies for socioeconomic and spatial equity with a data-driven approach can led governments to implement a more accessible service. Lastly, shared micromobility schemes must be analysed within the political and social context to assess potential opportunities for more equitable services.







References

———. 2025. “From Paper to Practice: Shared Micromobility Equity Policies Yield Mixed Outcomes.” Transportation Research Interdisciplinary Perspectives 31 (May): 101480. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trip.2025.101480.

Guan, Xiaodong, Dea van Lierop, Zihao An, Eva Heinen, and Dick Ettema. 2024. “Shared Micro-Mobility and Transport Equity: A Case Study of Three European Countries.” Cities 153 (October): 105298. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cities.2024.105298.


Su, Lin, Xiang Yan, and Xilei Zhao. 2024. “Spatial Equity of Micromobility Systems: A Comparison of Shared E-Scooters and Docked Bikeshare in Washington DC.” Transport Policy 145 (January): 25–36. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tranpol.2023.10.008.

title: Sustainable Spatial Planning and Analysis
text:
Active travel infrastructure in the Lima Metropolitan Area is characterized by a severe socio-spatial divide. While central districts benefit from connected cycle networks and flat terrain, peripheral areas endure a lack of infrastructure, steep topography, and high traffic stress (Guzman, Oviedo, and Rivera 2017). This report develops a Bikeability Index to quantify this inequity and evaluate proposed municipal cycling projects.



Figure 1: Study Area - Metropolitan Area of Lima

title: Transport Data Science
text:
Background and Objectives
In 2023, Cambridgeshire County Council introduced an active travel strategy to achieve net-zero carbon emissions by 2045, aligning with the 15-minute city framework. This report evaluates the spatial and socio-economic equity impacts of a 20-minute active travel strategy across the urban and peri-urban areas of Cambridge. The primary objectives are to develop a multimodal routing engine, identify areas lacking access to essential Points of Interest (POIs), and analyze the correlation between transport accessibility and social exclusion.



Figure 1: Study Area and PT Network




Methodology
The study defines its working area using a 5km buffer around the geometric center of Cambridge, discretizing the environment into a high-resolution 100-meter hexagonal grid.

The r5r package was utilized as the multimodal routing engine to calculate travel times for walking, cycling, and public transport modes.
The model integrates OpenStreetMap network and POI data, General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS) public transport schedules for the East Anglia region, and topographical elevation models.
Accessibility was measured against a strict 20-minute time threshold (utilizing a step decay function) to four equally weighted POI categories: healthcare, education, supermarkets, and leisure.
Scores were normalized using a min-max formula (\(x_{norm} = \frac{x - x_{min}}{x_{max} - x_{min}}\)) and aggregated to the Lower Super Output Area (LSOA) level to compare against the Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD).



Key Findings: Spatial Accessibility



Figure 2: Spatial accessibility analysis for different modes



The spatial analysis reveals significant disparities depending on the mode of transport analyzed:
While the city center enjoys the highest accessibility levels across all modes, public transport accessibility drops off sharply outside this central radius.
Cycling demonstrates a highly resilient and dispersed spatial pattern, maintaining strong accessibility levels outward into the peri-urban areas.
Increasing the public transport time threshold from 20 to 30 minutes improves coverage but still fails to close the accessibility gap when compared to the efficiency of the cycling network.



Key Findings: Socio-Economic Equity



Figure 3: Inaccessibility analysis for the 20-minute threshold



Aggregating the spatial data with 2025 IMD deciles uncovers distinct transport social exclusion trends.
There is a clear positive correlation between cycling accessibility and LSOA deprivation levels; the most deprived areas consistently exhibit the lowest active travel accessibility.
Conversely, public transport accessibility does not display a clear relationship with deprivation levels across the analyzed zones.
A significant proportion of the population residing in Cambridge’s peripheral and highly deprived areas remains completely excluded from accessing essential opportunities within 20 minutes.



Limitations and Policy Recommendations
The study acknowledges methodological limitations, including the use of theoretical GTFS timetables that ignore real-time congestion delays, the aggregation of data to LSOAs which can obscure micro-level neighborhood variations, and the omission of perceived safety factors (e.g., traffic stress) in the cycling index calculation.
To address the identified socio-spatial gap, local authorities are advised to implement targeted, data-driven interventions in peripheral and deprived zones. Recommended strategies include expanding bike-share schemes, physically improving active travel infrastructure, and enhancing public transport schedules to ensure equitable access across the entirety of Cambridge.

Air Quality Analysis in Edinburgh

title: Air Quality Policy Design and Evaluation
text:
Overview
Nitrogen dioxide (NO2) remains a critical air quality and public health challenge in UK urban centres, strongly linked to respiratory illness and driven primarily by localised road traffic emissions. This report analyses long-term air quality and meteorological data (2018–2025) across Edinburgh to evaluate the dispersion dynamics and source contributions of this pollutant. By examining the impact of local airflow processes and recent transport interventions—including the 2020 COVID-19 lockdown restrictions and the 2024 Low Emission Zone (LEZ)—this summary evaluates the efficacy of urban transport policies on localised NO2 concentrations.



Figure 1: Selected monitoring stations for analysis




Methodology
The study integrates air quality and meteorological data from four monitoring sites representing different exposure environments: Urban Traffic (Edinburgh Nicolson Street), Urban Background (Edinburgh St Leonards), Rural Background (Bush Estate), and the Edinburgh Airport meteorological station. Utilising the R-based ‘openair’ project framework, spatial subtraction analysis and deseasonalised trend analyses were conducted to separate the street-level pollution increment from city-wide and regional baselines, allowing for a precise evaluation of tailpipe emission behaviours within urban geometries.



Figure 2: Time Variation plot of NO2 in the three stations (2018 - 2025)





Figure 3: Wind Rose plot of Edinburgh (2018 - 2025) meteorological station




Key findings
The Skimming Regime Behaviour: The Urban Traffic site at Nicolson Street operates as a dense ‘street canyon’ with a height-to-width (H/W) ratio of approximately 1.0. Prevailing southwest winds fail to penetrate the street level, creating a “skimming flow” and a recirculating vortex that traps vehicular emissions directly within the pedestrian area.



Figure 4: Perpendicular flow regime in the Urban Traffic station – H/W = 1


Local Source Dominance: Spatial subtraction analysis demonstrates that the localised street increment constitutes the vast majority of NO2 concentrations. While regional and city-background contributions remained minor and stable over time, the street increment proved to be highly sensitive to local transport policies.



Figure 5: NO2 trends in the three stations (2018 - 2025)





Figure 6: O3 trends in the three stations (2018 - 2025)


Primary NO2 Fraction: An estimated primary f-NO2 fraction of 10-15% indicates a significant presence of diesel vehicles, heavy goods vehicles (HGVs), and buses. Notably, the implementation of the Edinburgh LEZ has already demonstrated a measurable reduction of the f-NO2 at the Urban Traffic site located within its boundary.



Figure 7: NO2/NOx estimated contribution from wmission ratios (Urban Traffic and Urban Background)




Policy Implications and limitations
While COVID-19 restrictions temporarily reduced local NO2 levels in 2020, achieving sustained compliance requires proactive and permanent traffic management. The analysis highlights that future policy must aggressively target localised vehicle emissions rather than relying on regional improvements.
It is recommended that the City of Edinburgh Council maintains and expands upon the active travel infrastructure developed during the pandemic (e.g., the ‘Spaces for People’ project). Future investments should prioritise road-space reallocation to suppress general traffic volumes, increase pedestrianisation, and improve public transit connectivity. Furthermore, the strict enforcement of the June 2024 LEZ—which specifically targets pre-Euro 6 diesel vehicles—is essential. The Council should also evaluate the potential expansion of the LEZ boundaries to further limit vehicles with high f-NO2 fractions.


Conclusions
Understanding local dispersion dynamics is critical for effective transport policy. The combination of dense urban street canyons and a reliance on diesel-heavy transport creates persistent pollution hotspots that regional interventions cannot resolve. To protect public health over the long term, Edinburgh must sustain its transition toward active travel and strictly enforce emission-based vehicular restrictions to maintain safe NO2 concentration levels within its most heavily trafficked corridors.

title: Transport Modelling
text:
Urban and transport planning in Delft faces a choice between a ‘compact city’ model (scenario S1), which seeks high-density development, and a ‘decentralisation’ model (scenario S2), which aims to reduce congestion by using peripheral traffic capacity. With forecasted population growth (0.75% annually) and economic expansion (1% annually), local authorities must decide whether to accommodate this demand within the existing areas and network of Delft or to approve a major decentralised development in two new residential and employment zones (Zones 24 and 25).
The modelling process relies on the principle of ‘derived demand’, as people travel to satisfy a requirement (Ortúzar and Willumsen, 2024), meaning transport is a consequence of the separation between daily activities. Traffic flows observed in this study are treated as a direct function of socio-economic attributes (such as residents, jobs, research, and education) assigned to each zone. The model assumes that drivers in 2030 will “select a route so as to minimize their personal travel time between the origin and destination” (Mannering, 2020) to reduce their individual generalised cost. This equilibrium state allows for a robust comparison of network performance.

title: Transport Modelling
text:
Methodology
The study uses OmniTRANS software to perform the Four Stage Model (FSM):

Trip generation: Zonal productions (\(P_i\)) and attractions (\(A_i\)) were calculated using linear regression equations based on four independent variables: residents, jobs, research, and education for 2017 and 2030.
Distribution and modal split: Gravity model parameters calibrated for the 2017 scenario were held constant for the 2030 scenarios.
Assignment: A car deterministic user equilibrium assignment was performed to simulate route choices and reduce generalised costs.

title: Transport Modelling
text:
Key Findings: Macroscopic Network Efficiency
Developing new zones brings an improvement in network efficiency. Scenario S1 results in a higher congested network with a system Vehicle Travel Time (VTT) of 39,788 hours compared to Scenario S2, which results in a reduction of VTT to 37,973 hours. This leads to a significant saving of 4.56% (around 1,815 vehicle-hours in the peak hour).
However, this improvement comes with a trade-off, because system Vehicle Kilometres Travelled (VKT) increases by 0.85% in Scenario S2 (from 466,647 to 470,635 km). Although this increase is small, it shows that decentralisation reduces congestion intensity in the city centre but increases trip distances required to access activities (Banister, 2007).

title: Transport Modelling
section: Key Findings: Spatial Redistribution of Flow
text:
Key Findings: Spatial Redistribution of Flow
By comparing flows generated in each scenario, it is possible to visualise the reorganisation of vehicular flows.



Figure 1: Flow difference plot (S2 - S1)



Relief in the City Centre
Blue bandwidths in the flow difference map demonstrate that Scenario S2 achieves its objective to relieve the city centre. By relocating future growth to newly developed zones, this scenario reduces traffic from the internal network of the city centre. For example, local roads like Kanaalweg and Provincialeweg show a reduction in flow, dropping by 42.38% and 37.60% respectively, relieving key arterial roads.


Utilisation of Highway Capacity
Red bandwidths indicate that traffic has not disappeared; instead, it has moved to the periphery. The A13 North freeway acts as the primary access corridor for new zones in Scenario S2, where traffic flow increases by 28.83% (from \(4,749\text{ veh/hr}\) to \(6,118\text{ veh/hr}\) in the peak hour). However, this increase is efficiently absorbed: the Volume Capacity Ratio (VCR) only increases from an underutilised 0.49 to 0.64. Consequently, the A4 North freeway improves: its VCR drops from a congested 1.01 down to 0.89.

title: Transport Modelling
text:
Limitations and Recommendations

Recommendation
Based on the evaluation of impacts in Delft, it is recommended that local authorities do not proceed with the new residential and employment land-use policy from Scenario S2.


Justification & Limitations

Baseline Comparison: Scenario S2 does not solve network congestion, providing only a slight improvement over Scenario S1. Average network speeds drop to \(12.39\text{ km/h}\) (an approximate 40% drop from 2017 conditions of \(20.47\text{ km/h}\)).
Temporary Relief: City centre relief is due to the displacement of residents to peripheral zones, risking uncontrolled urban growth and eventual peripheral gridlock.
Sustainable Consequences: Scenario S2 increases private car dependency, boosts system VKT by 0.85%, raises vehicle emissions, and induces irreversible demand.



Alternative and Complementary Suggestions

Polycentric Mixed-Use: Implement a polycentric mixed-use approach to create a better match between jobs and workers in urban space, mitigating excess commuting (Kim and Choi, 2019).
Modal Shift Investment: Redirect infrastructure budgets from peripheral land-use development into public transport and active travel improvements within the existing urban network, complemented by aggressive demand management (e.g., low emission zones, parking restrictions).

title: Sustainable Spatial Planning and Analysis
text:
Active travel infrastructure in the Lima Metropolitan Area is characterized by a severe socio-spatial divide. While central districts benefit from connected cycle networks and flat terrain, peripheral areas endure a lack of infrastructure, steep topography, and high traffic stress (Guzman, Oviedo, and Rivera 2017). This report develops a Bikeability Index to quantify this inequity and evaluate proposed municipal cycling projects.



Figure 1: Study Area - Metropolitan Area of Lima

title: Sustainable Spatial Planning and Analysis
text:
Methodology
The study employs a grid-based Spatial Multi-Criteria Analysis (SMCA) mapped over 100 x 100 m cells within Lima’s inhabited urban boundary. The index integrates five spatial variables, calculating localized values within a 250 m catchment buffer representing the average acceptable cycling detour (Krenn, Oja, and Titze 2015).
To create a unified Bikeability Index, the raw data for these five variables was categorized into a discrete 1 to 10 scale (where 10 indicates high bikeability) based on statistical deciles (Winters et al. 2013; Santos et al. 2022).

title: Sustainable Spatial Planning and Analysis
text:
Key Findings: The Socio-Spatial Gap
The resulting index reveals that optimal cycling conditions, defined as scores between 6 and 8, are heavily concentrated in the flat, well-connected ‘Centric Lima’ area. Conversely, urban peripheries present highly unfavorable environments for active travel modes due to moderate slopes and arterial road traffic.



Figure 3: Bikeability Index of the Metropolitan Area of Lima


By integrating 2021 population data, the severity of this inequity becomes quantifiable.

Approximately 63% of Lima’s residents live in areas with a Bikeability Index score below 4, facing compounding spatial barriers and a lack of connected infrastructure.
Only a minority of the population (around 12%) resides in areas considered accessible for cycling (scores of 6 to 8).

title: Sustainable Spatial Planning and Analysis
text:
Policy Implications & Limitations
An analysis of the Metropolitan Municipality of Lima’s future cycle infrastructure projects indicates a continued focus on improving connectivity within the already dense central districts. This approach will inadvertently continue to marginalise peripheral areas that possess high destination density (POIs) but lack dedicated infrastructure. The report recommends shifting from a coverage-based metric to an accessibility-based metric that prioritises these underserved peripheral zones.

title: Sustainable Spatial Planning and Analysis
text:
Conclusions
Finally, the report acknowledges methodological limitations (Arellana et al. 2020; Cervero et al. 2009; Lu, Sarkar, and Xiao 2018), most notably the exclusion of a personal safety variable. In the Latin American context, the perceived risk of street crime is a critical determinant in active travel behavior, which may negatively offset the benefits of segregated cycle lanes. Additionally, utilizing park area as an environmental proxy fails to account for the quality of shading and thermal comfort provided by trees.
